Secretary Kissinger has said maybe there are 175,000. Clearly there is no legal inhibition to bringing some out along with Americans, but 175,000, with American troops involved, could involve us in a very large war. This raises the specter of a new war, thousands of American troops holding on in an enclave for a long period.

[GF-2] It is not envisaged that this would be for a long period but as quickly and precisely as possible.

[JB-4] What concerns us is that a week ago Habib told us we would be formulating a plan. A week has gone by and nothing has happened. We should focus on getting them out. Getting the Vietnamese out and military aid for the GVN are totally different.

[HK-2] The plan for American evacuation is in pretty good shape. But we had a report that if we pulled out and left them in the lurch, we may have to fight the South Vietnamese. It was that we were concerned with and that is why we waited to go to Thieu so we didn't do it in the context of a bug out. The second problem is getting American citizens out in an emergency. Third is the Vietnamese to whom we have an obligation. This is infinitely more complicated and large-scale. It requires cooperation from the GVN and maybe the North Vietnamese.

[JB-4] I feel put upon in being presented an all or nothing number. I don't want to have to vote to buy it all or not at all. I am not sure I can vote for an amount to put American troops in for one to six months to get the Vietnamese out. I will vote for any amount for getting the Americans out. I don't want it mixed with getting the Vietnamese out.

[GF-2] There are three operations that are intertwined. There is getting out 4,500, the last 1,800 and the Vietnamese. The worst way to do it is to label it evacuation aid.

[SS-8] I am very familiar with Vietnam. In 1967 I decided it was hopeless. My people are asking if we are asking if we are holding Americans hostage for more aid. We know that is not so, but what worries me is the feeling we have been wrong so many times. We are all surprised at the collapse of South Vietnam. Why did we leave the 6,000 there so far? Where are the 175,000 going? Who is going to take them? These could all be dealt with if we could get the Americans out.

[CP-3] We could put these people in Borneo. It has the same latitude, the same climate, and would welcome some anti-Communists.

[GF-2] We opened our door to the Hungarians, I am not saying the situation is identical but our tradition is to welcome the oppressed. I don't think these people should be treated any differently from any other people -- the Hungarians, Cubans, Jews from the Soviet Union.

[RC-2] Is the request for military assistance primarily to arrest the situation and bring on negotiations, or for something else?

[GF-2] We wanted the sum to stabilize the military situation in order to give a chance for negotiations and to permit evacuation of Americans and deserving Vietnamese.

[JS-4] Do we have any obligations under the Paris Accords?

[GF-2] We signed with the understanding we could uphold it. The means were taken from us.

[JS-4] But our obligations....

[HK-2] The Accords had not obligations but authorities, that is, Article 7. President Nixon and others judged that permitting the United States to extricate itself would permit the United States to provide aid and enforce the agreements. Under the Paris Accords we have no obligation. To the GVN we said that if they let us get our forces out it would enhance our chances of getting aid for them and enforcing the agreement. It was in this context, not that of a legal obligation. We never claimed an obligation; we never pleaded an obligation. But some of us think there is a moral obligation.

[MM-4] My position is well known and I won't change. The caucus was concerned about the pace of the evacuation. Also that the witnesses should be the highest members of your Administration. We are trying to comply with your request as soon as possible. If Hugh [Scott] agrees, we will not meet Tuesday and Wednesday so we can process these requests rapidly. There was concern about humanitarian aid and the desire to send it through non-governmental agencies and the UN.

[HS-5] I agree to the proposal. One thing we haven't discussed is the amount. I think we need to discuss a figure.

[JB-4] I don't want to commit myself to any precise number. How much money depends on how many we try to get out.

[HK-2] This is a matter of extreme delicacy. We can't take them under crisis conditions. No one is thinking of a long period of time to get people out. We are thinking of ten days to two weeks.

[FC-2] I think we should establish an emergency fund to allow you to deal with the situation and carefully draw the language about troops so as to insure there are limits.

[GF-2] We are not wanting to put American troops in but we have to have enough funds to make it look like we plan to hold for some period.

[JJ-1] The idea here is very different from what I envisioned. I and most Senators thought of a surgical extraction, not of a ten-day to two-week operation with a bridgehead. This is a re-entry of a magnitude we have not envisioned. I think we have to keep this very quiet. I thought it was a one-shot airlift.

[CC-4] This was essential to have been said. The only way we could do an operation of this kind is through negotiations between the North and South.

[JJ-1] I can see North Vietnam deciding not to let us get these people out and attacking our bridgehead. Then we would have to send forces to protect our security force. That fills me with fear.

[JJ-3] Tell the press we are thinking of $200 million.

[GF-2] If this is a meeting to plan an evacuation, this will panic the GV totally.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Hi, Henry.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Hi. We had just a good WSAG meeting.2 You've really charged these guys up now.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Did we get some weather, did you say?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, we're getting some weather, but they are really pouring in naval ships now.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Did he [Moorer] get the point with it?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Oh.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Did you tell him about the--is he ready for a mining exercise?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He'll have a plan first thing in the morning. He said thank--tell the President--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Leak it.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: """"Not since '64""""--No, I'm--we're doing it even better. I've told him to start loading mines in the Philippines--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Good.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --on ships.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: How about--?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That will leak it.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: How about having--telling Helms. Did you tell him that?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yep, that's good.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Would you mind giving Helms the word that I--?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Helms, of course he's a bit of a whore, but he's thrilled. Now, Rush asked to see me yesterday, asking me to see me after the meeting. He said he reviewed the whole record. [RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And about giving the reports of--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yeah.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --both sides.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And also the request for authorities. You see, one reason I was so leery is they wanted to hit logistics and SAMs. Laird didn't approve it; he just wanted to hit SAMs. And to me the price just was too high for that.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Um-hmm.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, I just want you to know that. This thing--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: What is it? Have they got--they've gotten a little charged up then?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Oh, God. We--they're now. We have one question, I don't really--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --know whether I need to bother you with it. I think we ought to put in some more aircraft.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Well, where the hell is it?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, the choice is to move 36 Marine planes out of Japan or 54 from the United States Air Force. The Marines would have to--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Bring them--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --bring in 500 more people with them because of they don't have their ground support--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: They are to be stationed in--in this country--?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: In Da Nang--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: In-country? If we can do it--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: In order to move the Air Force out.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah. The Air Force thing is not considered to be an increase in our complement there, is it?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Not--no. Maybe a hundred people, but that would be--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --absorbed by the withdrawal.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: The Marines are better. The Marines will do a better job. Let's do whatever does a better job. What do you think?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: All right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: First you're going to raise more aircraft. Oh, the Air Force isn't that bad. Let's not [unclear]. We shouldn't blame those pilots; they're brave. The poor sons-of-bitches are all POWs and this and that. You know? They fought well. It's these goddamn airplanes that are no good.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, they're both using the same planes. Let me check with Haig who he thinks will do the better job.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: But would you give me it quickly? Would you say that--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --would you say, first, that Moorer is charged up now? Huh?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Absolutely. And the whole admiralty. I said, I repeated what you had said this morning. I said, """"The President said he doesn't want to be told about political campaigns or anything else. He has the responsibility for the security of this country. He has concluded that for us to be run out of Vietnam would undermine our foreign policy. And he has an obligation to do the right thing. So all you people are obliged to do is to tell him what the right thing is.""""4 And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Except pouring them in.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Except pouring them in. I said, """"Anything short of ground combat we want to do.""""

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: So what'd they say?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: """"There's not--you are responsible for telling all your subordinate commanders--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Um-hmm.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --that they should think of things to do."""" He said, """"God, I haven't heard""""--Moorer said, """"I haven't heard this since '63"""".

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Oh, yes. He's heard it from me.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: He forgets it.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yeah. And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Very well.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, they are now, they--they're moving 20 B-52s out there.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Good.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They've already moved 18 F-4s.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Good.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They are moving--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Are they moving another carrier?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, the other carrier they think would take too long.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: All right, fine.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And they'd have to move it--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: These four would be enough, probably.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: These four would be enough--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And how about the fleet? Can they get some more of them? Get some more than four destroyers? Let's put in--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, no. They've already--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --put in 100 destroyers.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They've already got 10 destroyers there; they're moving 8 more down, plus 3 cruisers. And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Well, that's a hell of a lot of firepower.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That is. And you remember these have 5-inch guns. And, I told him to start hitting logistics installations in Dong Hoi, to start hitting the airfield in Dong Hoi.5

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He said, """"Do you mean it?"""" I said, """"Of course we mean it.""""

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Is Dong Hoi an airfield? Can it be reached by, by this--?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yes.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Have we done it before?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Never.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: We haven't? Why not?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Because of the bombing understanding.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Oh, you mean we haven't. But it was done by Johnson, I presume?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right, but never by naval gunfire, because--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: The naval gunfire, it seems to me, would be better than bombing.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yeah. Oh, yeah. We should really pour it in there now.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Geez.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They'll scream like crazy. But I think--my view is this, Mr. President, this is not going to break open the war.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Your viewalso is, I think, correct, that we ought to delay a 48-hour strike because the weather has been bad.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Has there been any improvement in the weather? You say they got 200 strikes off. I hope that Moorer didn't go drop 'em over the boondocks--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, no--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --because of the number of strikes.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, no--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Goddamnit, that isn't what I was telling him.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I've talked to--I've talked to Moorer, incidentally. He thinks if we give him unlimited authority to hit up to the 18th parallel--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: --in other words, just extend it 5 more miles--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Do it!

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: He'd prefer that to the 48-hour strike all over South Vietnam.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: All right, fine.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And it gives us a better position because we can then say we're just supporting the immediate combat zone.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's right. We're supporting the combat zone and that's all.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And we can then, as we--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And then we can do more in a smaller--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That's right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --place.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That's right. And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And then also it's a signal to them we might do more later. Now, you see, the mining, though, will really be the--will really be the thing that'll tick them off. We've got to--I think that one has got to come--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But we should wait at least a week--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --quite soon. Quite soon. I'm not so sure we have to even wait. I'm not so sure [unclear]--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But it wouldn't take effect, Mr. President, for a month or two.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: I know, but you know we're in a position now where--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --a bold play is going to make the difference.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But I think, Mr. President, they've given us a chance. They threw down the gauntlet and if we now break them, if the South Vietnamese can form a line, this is beyond contention--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Did you tell Moorer about my theory about retreating?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: You see, I read again last night. I went back to, deliberately, and read Churchill's chapter about March 21st. And as you know, [Lieutenant General Sir Hubert de la Poer]Gough, a great one of the British military commanders, the hero of '16, was cashiered as a result of the damn thing. And then--and Churchill finally said it, it was a--and then he pointed out why it was a German defeat and a Brit--and an allied victory. He said for the first time in the war since Ypres, he said that the Germans lost 2 to 1 on the offensive in casualties to the British, and 3 to 2 in terms of officers. But look, but look--but look what it looked like, I mean what it looked like in terms of the battle. The Germans captured, Henry, in the first four days of that battle, they captured 60,000 British. Captured 60,000. Captured over a thousand heavy guns. They killed and wounded 200,000 British in the course of the day. And every body said, """"a great German victory."""" Ludendorff was whining. He [unclear] and it was a hell--and, as Churchill said, it was a defeat.6

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And we've got to--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Mr. President, I agree--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: But how--let me tell you, the other point that I, which I particularly noted, Churchill made the point of retreat. And he said, they kept going back, and they kept going back, and they gave up ground, but they won [laughs] the war. The hell with the ground! Unless it's--unless it's Hue, or--you know what I mean?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Hue and Da Nang you can't lose--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Did you--did you tell--did you tell him that? Has he--have they been figuring about a strategic retreat?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Yeah, I've told him, and of course, Thieu's interest, he doesn't want to lose any cities.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: All right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: We're trying to win the war--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I believe, Mr. President, if we can hold the line, as long as it doesn't mean the loss of Hue and Da Nang, if we can hold the line then we've got them out in the open where they are concentrated; there's no jungle there. And we are going to grind them down. And if they then have to withdraw north of the DMZ, Mr. President, we will be able to do to them politically what they did to us after Laos.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: They invaded and retreated?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: They invaded and retreated. No one will care how many casualties.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: The North Vietnamese--the South Vietnamese have got to attack--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --to drive them out.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And if we get that done, then we must offer a negotiation fairly quickly after that. And then we may be out of the war before the end of the year.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's irrelevant. [unclear] Henry, getting out the war before the end of the year doesn't make any difference from a political standpoint. If we're not out before the election, then I'll have [unclear]--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That's what I mean--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --can go on four years [unclear]--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: No, no. What I mean is before the election--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: --we can do the right thing--

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: I mean before--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: We've got to. We've got to, in terms of before the election, the only thing that is going to do us any good is to do it in June, before the Democratic Convention. That's when we have to have our big announcement, you know. That's why I say it. That's what we're talking about it here. So as to--It's the--the war is not the problem; it is the issue that is the problem. You see my point?

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Right.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And the main thing is to have this battle now in B-1 [Front], where we kick the stuffings out of the bastards.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: So, that they can't come--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: And win one.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: And, so that they can't come back before the end of the year.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: That's right.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger:But before the election--

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: But I think that in terms of the--but I think that in terms of the negotiation, if this battle moves fairly fast, if there's any chance for it to move, if the weather breaks, my guess is that you'll have your negotiation quite soon.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That's what I think.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: [unclear]

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: That's what I think. That's exactly my opinion.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: When will the Warsaw thing be announced?7

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: Well, that will take us a week to announce--five days. We've notified them today. We've notified State to notify Warsaw. Of course, it came in through Warsaw channels, not through State channels.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Hang on.

[HENRY-KISS] Kissinger: But the major thing is not to tell Laird he did right. Well, not to tell him he did wrong, either. Just have him forget about the past. The major thing is to get this battle won.

[RICHARD-NI] Nixon: Yeah.

[JS-1] The Birch Society Congressmen are starting to work against Defense on economic grounds. I am going hopefully to join the Democratic study group. Dick Bolling I think can be good.

[GF-2] Bolling is good. Ullman is also good.

[JS-1] I think we will do all right in the House. Even Joe Biden is getting educated.

[GF-2] Virginia has a lot of Defense installations.

[JS-1] Do you mind if I close some of them after the elections?

[GF-2] No. Which ones?

[JS-1] The toughest is the Frankford Arsenal. Bhas been kept open because of Hugh Scott for 15 years.

[GF-2] How big is it?

[JS-1] About 5,000 people. It is old and the mission is obsolete. The personnel are ill trained. I also proposed the Pueblo Arsenal. Senator Dominick called and asked me to keep it open until after November.

[GF-2] What is its mission?

[JS-1] It is a depot. We have gone down from 6.3 million to 2.1 million people without shrinking the base structure. One is in McFall's and one is in Leggett's District. We must shrink the Army system so we can get to 16 divisions. It has long been overblown.

[GF-2] Military bases?

[JS-1] Fort Dix is the biggest one.

[GF-2] Clifford Case hasn't helped us.

[JS-1] He is okay on conventional forces. He's a frail reed, but he hasn't been too bad. We just don't need all the training facilities. We are also closing Fort Monroe.

[GF-2] Can you show the cost-to-benefit ratio?

[JS-1] Yes. They have cut manpower by 30,000. I can take that without cutting strength. We will consolidate the two in California in McFall' district rather than in Leggetts, though it will cost one-half million more.

[GF-2] We won't have closings to help someone else. I heard an Army Base closed in Omaha and one opened in Louisiana. If you have to move, ok, but don't do it to help people out.

[JS-1] I stopped the Navy from moving Suitland to Mississippi. Stennis is very nervous. Pastore wanted it moved to Rhode Island. The Navy wanted to help Stennis.

[GF-2] These districts who forgot to get bases are in the long run better off. I didn't try to get any. It is a snare and a delusion. It's much too uncertain.

[JS-1] I agree. The facilities in Mendel Rivers' district are slipping away. But I need your support with Scott, He is a patriot.

[GF-2] On any of these, get me a 10-page paper showing all the background. Hugh is a statesman if you show common sense and political savvy.

[JS-1] I hope Dominick pulls through. The AFL-CIO said they wouldn't forget Milton Young.

[GF-2] Milton Young is very good. It's just his age. How can the AFL -- with Meany's strength - support Hart in Colorado? Pete [Dominick] needs all the help he can get.

[JS-1] The problem is Hart is going moderate.

[GF-2] The strange race is in South Dakota. Thorsness is likable.

[JS-1] McGovern is actually a moderate.

[GF-2] I'm hearing Javits is in trouble.

[JS-1] I think he's o.k. I will talk to the AFL about it. The Democrats have done well in the Governor races -- a moderate does better than a radical. But they can't do that in a Senate race unless they can get the Jews.

[GF-2] The Cuba trip didn't help him. I am worried about tank production.

[JS-1] It's a big problem. Basically the marginal foundries are being put out of business by the environmental laws.

[GF-2] If you had your druthers, how much would you increase it?

[JS-1] From 260 to 1200. And despite all this Stratton isn't satisfied at Water Vliet. We make gun turrets there. We have trouble if we give 200 tanks to Israel. The Saudis complained they had to wait two years and Israel gets it right away.

[GF-2] If you started now, how long would it take to get going?

[JS-1] We're up to about 500 now; I had hoped to be to 800. But I am out of foundries and may have to get them in Germany.

[GF-2] Who builds them? And how much do they cost?

[JS-1] About 35,000. Chrysler does it in an old World-War II plant.

[GF-2] Rhodes was after me to get some government-owned foundry on the market so GM could move in. If Congress cut us $7 billion from $304 billion and the Department of Defense had to cut short, where would you get it?

[JS-1] I would cut civil service. But O & M is the only way to get it quickly. I probably would have to cut Navy overseas deployment -- in the Mediterranean, for example.

[GF-2] This would given an excuse to close those facilities. Would you cut military or civilians?

[JS-1] I would slow recruitment, but wouldn't reduce end strength. We took a cut in O & M this year. I told you everything looked like $96 billion in '76 outlays. It now looks like $95 billion. We are very thin on strength. You can keep current levels. We are at 5.6% of GNP as compared to 9.6% ten years ago. We can't keep on doing this and stay second to none. FY '75 spending will be between $83 and $84 billion.

[GF-2] Where will the cuts come?

[JS-1] From slowing procurement. The problem is we are coming into a lot of procurement from prior years. Inflation has cost us $9 billion. To repair the Department we have to face up to the costs. I told Ullman our defense strengths in proportion to the share of GNP.

[GF-2] Can't DOD help us over NPR No. 1 and No. 4? Number 1 would be very helpful now. Why won't Eddie go along?

[JS-1] I think a deal is possible. Number 4 is tougher than Number 1. I think you can't with 750 million go into a production base in Number 4 in terms of developing national resources. It would worry the producers.

[GF-2] You mean if we prove out Number 4 that that would ease the pressure on Number 1?

[JS-1] No. We would continue to have resistance on production from Number 1.

[GF-2] Everyone on the California delegation is after me. They know the alternative is drilling in the channel. Can we get a deal with Eddie?

[JS-1] We will work on it. Vinson advised Hebert against it unequivocally.

[GF-2] I don't understand. It could help us right away.

[JS-1] Conservation for the Navy is a secular religion going back to Pinchot.

[GF-2] With the Navy going nuclear, how can they need more oil than 20 years ago?

[JS-1] It's not rational, just conservative. We are sending you a revised Unified Command Plan. It leaked and was embarrassing, in that it has been given to Bunker as a goodie in his negotiations.

[GF-2] Are the Panamanians against it?

[JS-1] Yes. SOUTHCOM does serve a useful purpose politically. It was proposed in '70 and rejected. Haig and Walters were opposed. On political grounds JCS now support it. I think it will get no support on the Hill.

[GF-2] Will PACOM take it over?

[JS-1] No. We would have forces take over the headquarters. It mostly handles MAP and we can do it from Washington. It is a colonial vestige. We also want to eliminate ALCAN. That is a Ted Stevens problem. It would become part of CONAD. It's the only state having a separate defense command. They still worry about World War I. I can put 5 divisions into Alaska in five days. I think we can swing it if we can have a 3-star flag there. We just can't afford these luxuries anymore.

[WILLIAM-CL] William P. Clark: Judge Clark opened the meeting by describing the importance of the Defense Guidance as the planning tool for the services as they prepare the FY85 defense budgets and then introduced Secretary Weinberger.

[CASPAR-WEI] Secretary Weinberger: The Secretary provided a twenty minute briefing of the Defense Guidance. This briefing included a description of the purpose of the Defense Guidance and its role in the DOD PPBS budget cycle. He stated that the Soviet threat policy guidance provided by the President and top-line budget ceilings formed the parameters for the Defense Guidance. He then highlighted comparisons of U. S. /Soviet procurement trends pointing out that if the Defense Guidance was not fully funded the asymmetries between U. S. and Soviet forces would increase.

[RONALD-REA] The President: The President said that it was important to make this force comparison known to the public. He suggested that a presentation of year-by-year comparative force strength growth would be very useful as a part of a public affairs effort to demonstrate the need for the defense program.

[CASPAR-WEI] Secretary Weinberger: The Secretary continued with a description of the resource allocation priorities which were reflected in the Defense Guidance. These include the need to maximize the quality of U. S. forces and improve the industrial base. Steps necessary to realize this goal included modernization of strategic nuclear forces and general purpose force capabilities readiness sustainability modernization force structure growth. The Secretary then described the Defense Guidance in terms of budget allocation for mission category. He noted that mission capabilities will increase 77% by FY88. The largest improvements will occur in mobility force and strategic capabilities. Specific strategic and conventional force improvements were highlighted. The briefing concluded with a discussion of how U. S. force capabilities to operate in Europe and Southwest Asia would improve by FY89 as a result of the Defense Guidance. The Secretary emphasized that achieving the force posture described in the Defense Guidance required successful funding of the FY84 request.

[ROBERT-BAR] General Barrow: The General offered the view of the JCS that the Defense Guidance was a good product which reflected the Services' desire to expose the U. S. to the least possible risk given resource constraints. He noted that the various CINCs and Unified Commands had been given the opportunity to comment on the Defense Guidance throughout its preparation.

[RONALD-REA] The President: The President thanked the Secretary and General Barrow for their views and expressed the opinion that the specific detailed nature of the Defense Guidance refutes the criticism that the Administration has no overall strategic plan.

[ROBERT-BAR] General Barrow: The General emphasized that the Services felt that the improvements specified in the Defense Guidance were vital and that it represented a balanced and realistic program. If funded it would provide us with better quality forces than the Soviets. He added that the quality of U. S. military manpower was a key factor underlying the plan.

[RONALD-REA] The President: The President commented on the latest propaganda threat that he was aware of -a film by anti-nuclear advocate Helen Caldicott noting that it represents the type of criticism to which U. S. security planning is continually subjected to.

[WILLIAM-CL] Judge Clark: The Judge asked Secretary Weinberger if there were any plans to reduce the number of aircraft carriers which had been cited in previous Defense Guidance documents. He asked whether there was any change in the goal of a 600-ship Navy.

[CASPAR-WEI] Secretary Weinberger: The Secretary indicated that there were no plans to do this and that the target for carrier battle groups remained at 15. Two carriers were funded last year although there were Congressmen who advocated cutting one. Such action would cost us 22 months in additional time to achieve two new carriers and an extra $750 million. He indicated that differing accounts about the carrier force goal reflected the fact that older carriers would be taken from active service as they entered the ship life extension program.

[DAVID-STOC] Mr. Stockman: Mr. Stockman requested a briefing in the future which would describe how the DOD arrives at the force structure goals seven divisions to Europe in seven weeks etc.

[CASPAR-WEI] Secretary Weinberger: The Secretary said that such determinations are based on an assessment of Soviet threat capabilities and plausible war scenarios. These analyses result in a force requirement sufficient to block any aggression until reinforcements are available.

[JEANE-KIRK] Ambassador Kirkpatrick: The Ambassador emphasized the importance of getting the real story about the national threat to Congress and the public. She repeated her belief that a major speech by the President on this subject was essential. She also suggested that a paid advertisement campaign funded by the Republican National Committee be considered. She said the key was to put the anti-defense lobby on the defensive.

[RONALD-REA] The President: The President agreed and emphasized that a new approach was necessary. He said that it was important to go beyond just discussing numbers and talk about the threat to U. S. security goals. He said that we needed specific examples of how the threat to U. S. security was growing (for example citing global chokepoints) to better illustrate the problem.

[WILLIAM-CL] Judge Clark: Judge Clark mentioned the effort to put together a public affairs strategy for the defense budget which is being headed by Mr. William Greener. He said that Mr. Greener had developed an extensive plan for presenting the rationale for the defense program which included special briefings and a speakers' program. Secretary Weinberger Secretary Weinberger agreed that the Greener effort would be an important addition to the goal of increasing Congressional and public support for the defense program.
